name: Teddy Bear
visual_anchor: A soft golden-brown teddy bear with a red bow tie sitting on a cozy patterned quilt beside a bedside lamp, warm bedtime glow, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Soft, cuddly toy many kids hug at bedtime
Usually stuffed and covered in fuzzy fabric
Shaped like a friendly round-eared forest animal
Named after a United States president's nickname

facts_and_myths.claim: The teddy bear is named after President Theodore Roosevelt.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Roosevelt's nickname was Teddy, and a 1902 cartoon about him and a bear inspired toymakers.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Around the same time, a German toy company called Steiff also began making stuffed toy bears.

facts_and_myths.claim: Teddy bears are named after a famous real bear called Teddy.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The name comes from President Theodore Roosevelt, not from any real bear.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Teddy bears became so popular in the early 1900s that they were sold all over the world.

name: Yo-Yo
visual_anchor: A shiny bright blue yo-yo spinning at the end of its string below a child's hand, sunny park background softly blurred, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Small toy that goes down and comes back up
Made of two discs joined by a short axle
A string is looped around the middle and tied to your finger
Famous tricks include Walk the Dog and Around the World

facts_and_myths.claim: A yo-yo has been played with in outer space.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In 1985, astronauts took a yo-yo on the Space Shuttle to show how toys behave without gravity.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In space, a yo-yo will not sleep at the bottom of its string the way it does on Earth.

facts_and_myths.claim: The yo-yo was first invented in the 1900s.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Yo-yo-like toys were played with in ancient Greece more than two thousand years ago.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Old Greek vases show children playing with disc toys on strings.

name: Spinning Top
visual_anchor: A colorful striped wooden spinning top twirling on a polished wooden floor, motion swirls of red, yellow and blue, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Toy that twirls around and around on one point
Often shaped like a cone or an upside-down pear
You twist it with your fingers or pull a string to start it
Wobbles and topples over when it slows down

facts_and_myths.claim: Spinning tops are one of the oldest toys in the world.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Archaeologists have found ancient tops made of clay and wood in many parts of the world.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A dreidel, spun during Hanukkah celebrations, is a kind of spinning top with four sides.

facts_and_myths.claim: A top falls over sooner the faster it spins.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Fast spinning actually keeps a top upright. It wobbles and falls as it slows down.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The same spinning balance helps a bicycle wheel stay upright while rolling.

name: Slinky
visual_anchor: A shiny metal coil spring toy stepping down a set of carpeted stairs in a graceful arch, bright cheerful living room, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Stretchy toy that can step down stairs by itself
Made from one long coiled band of metal or plastic
Makes a soft slinking sound when you pass it hand to hand
Invented in the 1940s after an engineer saw a spring fall

facts_and_myths.claim: A Slinky can walk down stairs all by itself.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Once you tip it over the first step, gravity and the coil's springiness keep it flipping down.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Slinky is the official state toy of Pennsylvania.

facts_and_myths.claim: When you drop a hanging Slinky, the bottom starts falling right away.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The bottom seems to hover for a moment until the collapsing top coils reach it.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Slow-motion cameras made this floating Slinky trick famous with science fans.

name: Kaleidoscope
visual_anchor: A child holding a painted tube up to one eye while a bright snowflake-like pattern of colored jewels glows in a circle beside them, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Tube toy you look into and turn
Shows changing patterns of bright colors
Uses mirrors inside to repeat shapes like a snowflake
Invented by a Scottish scientist in the 1810s

facts_and_myths.claim: The kaleidoscope was invented by Scottish scientist David Brewster.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Brewster created it in 1816 while studying how light reflects, and it quickly became a hit.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The name comes from Greek words meaning beautiful shape to look at.

facts_and_myths.claim: The patterns inside a kaleidoscope are painted pictures.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Loose beads or glass bits are reflected by angled mirrors, creating new patterns each turn.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: You almost never see the exact same kaleidoscope pattern twice.

name: Jack-in-the-Box
visual_anchor: A smiling clown puppet with a striped hat popping up on a spring from a colorful painted box, confetti in the air, playful nursery, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A box toy with a surprise inside
You turn a crank on the side and music plays
At the end of the song, the lid flies open
A smiling figure on a spring pops out

facts_and_myths.claim: Many jack-in-the-boxes play the song Pop Goes the Weasel.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The figure usually jumps out right on the word pop at the end of the tune.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The pop-out figure is often a clown or jester.

facts_and_myths.claim: A jack-in-the-box needs batteries to make its figure pop out.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A squeezed spring inside the box pushes the figure out when the latch releases.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Jack-in-the-box toys have been surprising kids for hundreds of years.

name: Rocking Horse
visual_anchor: A dapple-gray wooden rocking horse with a red saddle and flowing mane in a sunny playroom, toys scattered on a rug, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Toy animal a child can sit on and ride
Moves back and forth but never goes anywhere
Has a saddle, a mane and often a real-looking tail
Stands on curved wooden runners or a sliding stand

facts_and_myths.claim: Some rocking horses glide on a stand instead of curved rockers.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The stand keeps the horse from tipping too far or creeping across the floor.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Before rocking horses, kids rode hobby horses: a stick with a horse head on top.

facts_and_myths.claim: Rocking horses were invented only after plastic toys appeared.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Wooden rocking horses were popular toys in Europe hundreds of years before plastic.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Many old rocking horses had manes and tails made from real horsehair.

name: Building Blocks
visual_anchor: A tall tower of bright red, blue, yellow and green wooden blocks stacked on a sunny playroom rug, a few blocks tumbling at the side, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Simple shapes you stack to build things
Often cubes, arches and cylinders made of wood
Some have letters or numbers on their sides
Used in early kindergartens to teach shapes and balance

facts_and_myths.claim: The inventor of kindergarten used blocks to help young children learn.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Friedrich Froebel gave children wooden blocks in the 1800s to explore shapes and numbers.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Kindergarten is a German word meaning children's garden.

facts_and_myths.claim: A wider base makes a block tower easier to knock over.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A wide base makes a tower steadier. Narrow towers tip over more easily.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Real skyscrapers are also designed to be steady and strong at their base.

name: Toy Train Set
visual_anchor: A bright red toy steam train pulling colorful carriages around an oval track past tiny trees and a little station, cozy playroom floor, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A small engine and cars that run around a track
Tracks can loop, cross bridges and pass tiny stations
Some run on electricity, others are pushed or wound up
Comes in sizes called scales, such as HO and O

facts_and_myths.claim: HO scale model trains are about 87 times smaller than real trains.
facts_and_myths.explanation: HO is one of the most popular model train sizes, built at a scale of 1 to 87.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Some early electric toy trains were made to attract shoppers to store windows.

facts_and_myths.claim: Every toy train needs electricity to move.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Many toy trains are pushed by hand, wound up with a key, or pulled along.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Wooden push-along train sets are popular with toddlers around the world.

name: Rag Doll
visual_anchor: A sweet cloth doll with red yarn hair, button eyes and a patchwork dress sitting in a small wicker chair by a sunny window, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Soft doll you can hug and carry anywhere
Made from fabric scraps and stuffed with cotton or rags
Often has yarn hair and stitched or button eyes
A famous one named Raggedy Ann appeared over 100 years ago

facts_and_myths.claim: Raggedy Ann is one of the most famous rag dolls ever made.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Writer Johnny Gruelle created her in 1915 and later wrote storybooks about her adventures.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Raggedy Ann has a twin brother doll named Raggedy Andy.

facts_and_myths.claim: Rag dolls are a fairly new kind of toy.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Cloth dolls are among the oldest toys. Some found by archaeologists date to Roman times.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Families often sewed rag dolls at home from leftover scraps of cloth.

name: Marbles
visual_anchor: A handful of shiny swirled glass marbles in blue, green and orange rolling across a chalk circle on a sunny sidewalk, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Small round balls that roll and clink
Usually made of colorful swirled glass
Players flick them to knock others out of a circle
The bigger one you flick with is called a shooter

facts_and_myths.claim: Marbles are a choking hazard for children under three years old.
facts_and_myths.explanation: They are small enough to block a little throat, so keep them away from babies and toddlers.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A marble with a colored swirl shaped like an eye is called a cat's eye.

facts_and_myths.claim: Marbles have always been made of glass.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Early marbles were made of clay, stone or wood. Glass marbles became common later.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Marbles got their name because some were once made from marble stone.

name: Wind-Up Toy
visual_anchor: A shiny tin robot toy with a big silver key on its back marching across a wooden table, little gears glinting, cheerful bright light, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Toy that moves on its own after you twist it
Has a little key or knob on its back or side
A coiled spring inside slowly unwinds to power it
Classic examples include chattering teeth and marching robots

facts_and_myths.claim: Turning the key of a wind-up toy tightens a spring inside.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The tight spring stores energy, then slowly unwinds to turn gears and move the toy.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Old mechanical clocks and watches use the same kind of wound-up spring.

facts_and_myths.claim: Wind-up toys need batteries to move.
facts_and_myths.explanation: They run purely on spring power, so no batteries or plugs are needed.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Many wind-up toys were made from colorful printed tin.

name: Jigsaw Puzzle
visual_anchor: A half-finished jigsaw puzzle of a colorful hot air balloon scene on a wooden table, loose interlocking pieces scattered nearby, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A picture broken into many small pieces
Pieces have knobs and holes that lock together
Many people start by finding the flat-edged border pieces
The first ones were maps cut up to teach geography

facts_and_myths.claim: The first jigsaw puzzles were maps used to teach geography.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In the 1760s, London mapmaker John Spilsbury glued a map to wood and cut out the countries.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Early puzzles were cut by hand, so each one was a little bit different.

facts_and_myths.claim: Every jigsaw puzzle piece has four knobs sticking out.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Pieces mix knobs and holes, and edge pieces have at least one flat side.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Corner pieces have two flat sides, which makes them easy to spot.

name: Paper Airplane
visual_anchor: A crisp white folded paper airplane gliding through a bright blue sky over a green schoolyard, soft clouds behind, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A toy you can make from a single sheet of paper
Folded into a pointy nose and two flat wings
Glides through the air after a gentle throw
Small changes to the folds change how it flies

facts_and_myths.claim: Bending the back edges of the wings changes how a paper airplane flies.
facts_and_myths.explanation: These small flaps work like the elevators on real planes, tilting the nose up or down.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The world record paper airplane flight is longer than half a soccer field.

facts_and_myths.claim: Heavier paper always makes a paper airplane fly farther.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Too much weight makes it drop fast. Good folds and balance matter more.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Real engineers sometimes use paper airplanes to explain how wings create lift.

name: Origami Crane
visual_anchor: A bright pink folded paper crane with pointed wings perched on a table beside a string of rainbow paper cranes, soft daylight, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A paper model of a long-necked bird
Folded from one square sheet with no cutting
Comes from the Japanese art of paper folding
A string of one thousand is a wish for good luck

facts_and_myths.claim: In Japan, folding one thousand paper cranes is a wish for good luck.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A string of a thousand cranes, called senbazuru, is given as a hopeful gift for health and happiness.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The word origami comes from Japanese words meaning fold and paper.

facts_and_myths.claim: You need scissors and glue to make an origami crane.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A classic origami crane is made only by folding one square of paper.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In Japan, the crane is a symbol of long life and good fortune.

name: Nesting Dolls
visual_anchor: A row of brightly painted wooden nesting dolls from biggest to tiniest, rosy cheeks and flowered scarves, on a sunny windowsill, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Set of wooden dolls in different sizes
Each doll opens in the middle
A smaller doll hides inside each bigger one
First made in Russia around 1890

facts_and_myths.claim: The first Russian nesting doll set had eight dolls.
facts_and_myths.explanation: It was carved and painted around 1890, with the smallest doll as a tiny baby.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Nesting dolls won a medal at the 1900 World's Fair in Paris.

facts_and_myths.claim: Russian nesting dolls are an ancient toy thousands of years old.
facts_and_myths.explanation: They were first made in the 1890s, which is fairly recent for a classic toy.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The idea may have been inspired by a set of nesting dolls from Japan.

name: Kite
visual_anchor: A bright diamond-shaped kite in red and yellow with a long ribbon tail soaring high above a grassy hill on a breezy blue-sky day, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Flies high in the sky on a windy day
Held by a long string from the ground
Often diamond-shaped with a fluttering tail
First flown in China more than two thousand years ago

facts_and_myths.claim: Kites should never be flown near power lines.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A kite string touching power lines is very dangerous. Fly in open fields with an adult.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The city of Weifang in China is famous for its huge international kite festival.

facts_and_myths.claim: Kites fly best on days with no wind at all.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Kites need moving air to push them up. A steady gentle breeze works best.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Kites were invented in China long before paper airplanes or real airplanes.

name: Jump Rope
visual_anchor: A smiling child mid-jump over a swinging bright pink rope on a sunny playground, sneakers in the air, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Rope you swing over your head and hop over
Often has a handle at each end
Kids chant rhymes while jumping in time
A team game uses two ropes turning in opposite directions

facts_and_myths.claim: Double Dutch is jump rope played with two ropes at once.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Two turners swing two ropes in opposite directions while a jumper hops between them.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Boxers often jump rope in training to get quick on their feet.

facts_and_myths.claim: Jumping rope is just a game, not real exercise.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Jumping rope is great exercise for your heart, legs and balance.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Many athletes use a jump rope to warm up before practice.

name: Hula Hoop
visual_anchor: A happy child spinning a bright rainbow-striped hoop around their waist on a sunny green lawn, motion blur on the hoop, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A big plastic ring you twirl around your body
You keep it spinning by moving your hips
Can also spin on arms, legs or necks
Became a giant craze in the late 1950s

facts_and_myths.claim: Children played with hoops long before plastic hula hoops existed.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Kids in ancient times rolled and twirled hoops made from wood, vines or metal.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In 1958, plastic hula hoops became so popular that millions sold in just a few months.

facts_and_myths.claim: To hula hoop, you must swing your hips in big circles.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A steady forward-and-back push with your hips keeps the hoop spinning best.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Bigger, heavier hoops spin more slowly, which makes them easier for beginners.

name: Flying Disc
visual_anchor: A bright orange plastic flying disc sailing through the air toward a leaping happy dog in a sunny green park, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Round, flat toy you throw with a flick of the wrist
Glides and floats through the air while spinning
Dogs love to leap and catch it
Used in a team sport called Ultimate

facts_and_myths.claim: Spinning helps a flying disc stay steady in the air.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The spin keeps the disc flat and stable, while its curved shape helps it float.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: College students once tossed empty metal pie tins for fun before plastic discs.

facts_and_myths.claim: The Frisbee was named after the person who invented it.
facts_and_myths.explanation: It was named after the Frisbie Pie Company, whose pie tins students tossed around.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: An early plastic flying disc was called the Pluto Platter.

name: Soap Bubbles
visual_anchor: A child blowing a cloud of shimmering rainbow soap bubbles from a plastic wand in a sunny garden full of flowers, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Floating see-through balls that pop when touched
Made by blowing soapy water through a wand
Shimmer with swirling rainbow colors
A super-thin skin of soap and water holds in the air

facts_and_myths.claim: Soap bubbles show rainbow colors because their skin is extremely thin.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Light bounces off the inside and outside of the thin film, creating shifting colors.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In freezing weather, soap bubbles can turn into fragile frozen crystal balls.

facts_and_myths.claim: Bubbles are round only because the wand is round.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Even square wands make round bubbles. A sphere holds air using the least skin.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: When bubbles touch each other, they press together and form flat walls.

name: Sandcastle
visual_anchor: A tall sandcastle with towers, a moat and a tiny flag on a sunny beach, colorful bucket and spade beside it, gentle waves behind, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Something you build at the beach
Shaped with a bucket, spade and your hands
Often has towers, walls and a moat
Waves at high tide can wash it away

facts_and_myths.claim: Damp sand sticks together much better than dry sand.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Tiny bits of water form bridges between sand grains, holding them together like glue.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Expert sand sculptors pack wet sand into forms to build huge, detailed castles.

facts_and_myths.claim: Dry sand is the best kind for building sandcastles.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Dry sand just slides and crumbles. Add some water, but not so much that it turns soupy.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Digging too deep in sand is unsafe because holes can cave in, so keep holes shallow.

name: Snowman
visual_anchor: A cheerful snowman with a carrot nose, coal-dark button eyes, a red knitted scarf and stick arms in a snowy front yard, soft snowflakes falling, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Built outside on a snowy winter day
Made by rolling big balls and stacking them
Often has a carrot nose and stick arms
Melts away when the weather warms up

facts_and_myths.claim: Slightly wet snow is the best kind for building a snowman.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Damp packing snow sticks together, so the balls grow bigger as you roll them.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In Japan, the traditional snowman is made from just two snowballs instead of three.

facts_and_myths.claim: Very cold, fluffy powder snow is perfect for rolling snowballs.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Powdery snow is too dry to stick, so it crumbles instead of rolling into a ball.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Snowmen often melt faster on sunny days, even when the air stays cold.

name: Sidewalk Chalk
visual_anchor: Chunky sticks of pastel sidewalk chalk next to a colorful drawing of a sun, rainbow and flowers on a sunny driveway, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Thick colorful sticks for drawing outdoors
Used to draw on pavement and driveways
Kids use it to draw hopscotch courts
Rain washes the drawings away

facts_and_myths.claim: Natural chalk rock is made from shells of tiny sea creatures.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Over millions of years, tiny ocean shells piled up and hardened into soft white rock.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The famous White Cliffs of Dover in England are made of chalk.

facts_and_myths.claim: Sidewalk chalk drawings stay on the ground forever.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Chalk sits on top of the pavement, so rain or a hose washes it away.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Draw away from roads and driveways where cars move, and ask an adult where it's safe.

name: Hopscotch
visual_anchor: A child hopping on one foot along a numbered chalk grid of colorful squares on a sunny playground, a small pebble in one square, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A hopping game drawn on the ground
Uses a row of numbered squares, often in chalk
You toss a small stone into a square and hop past it
Some squares need one foot and others need two

facts_and_myths.claim: In hopscotch, you must skip the square with your marker in it.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Players hop over the marked square, then pick up the marker on the way back.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Hopscotch is played all around the world with many different court shapes.

facts_and_myths.claim: Hopscotch got its name because it was invented in Scotland.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Scotch here is an old word for a scratched line, like the lines of the court.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: All you need to play hopscotch is chalk and a small stone or beanbag.

name: Pogo Stick
visual_anchor: A child wearing a bright helmet bouncing high on a red pogo stick on a sunny driveway, sneakers on the foot pegs, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Lets you bounce up and down while standing
A pole with handles on top and foot pegs below
A spring inside squeezes and pushes you back up
Riders should wear a helmet for safety

facts_and_myths.claim: A pogo stick uses a spring to store and release energy.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Your weight squeezes the spring as you land, and it pushes back to launch you up.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Extreme pogo sticks use air or rubber bands and can launch riders several meters high.

facts_and_myths.claim: A pogo stick needs a motor to make you bounce.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Pogo sticks are powered by your own jumps and a spring, with no motor at all.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Wearing a helmet and practicing on flat ground makes pogo riding safer.

name: Tricycle
visual_anchor: A shiny red tricycle with a white seat and streamers on the handlebars parked on a sunny sidewalk lined with flowers, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A small ride-on with pedals for young kids
Has one wheel in front and two in back
Stays up without the rider needing to balance
Many have pedals attached straight to the front wheel

facts_and_myths.claim: A tricycle stays upright even when it is not moving.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Three wheels make a steady base, so little riders don't need to balance.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In the 1880s, many grown-ups rode tricycles because tall early bicycles were hard to balance.

facts_and_myths.claim: A tricycle can never tip over.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Fast, sharp turns or steep slopes can tip a tricycle, so ride slowly and wear a helmet.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Some grown-ups still ride big three-wheeled bikes with baskets for shopping.

name: Hide and Seek
visual_anchor: A giggling child peeking out from behind a big leafy tree in a sunny backyard while another child counts with eyes covered, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A game of finding friends who are out of sight
One player covers their eyes and counts out loud
Everyone else quickly finds a place to hide
The seeker often shouts Ready or not, here I come

facts_and_myths.claim: There is a Hide and Seek World Championship for grown-ups.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Teams from many countries have competed in this playful contest held in Italy.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Hide and seek is played by children in almost every country on Earth.

facts_and_myths.claim: A fridge or car trunk is a safe place to hide.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Things that latch shut can trap you. Never hide inside fridges, trunks or chests.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The best hiding spots are safe ones where you can still breathe fresh air and get out.

name: Playground Slide
visual_anchor: A child happily zooming down a bright yellow twisty slide in a sunny playground, wood chips below and trees behind, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: You climb up a ladder and whoosh down
Has a smooth sloping surface with raised sides
Can be straight, wavy, twisty or shaped like a tube
Gravity pulls you down while smoothness keeps you sliding

facts_and_myths.claim: Metal slides can get hot enough in summer sun to hurt skin.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Sunlight heats metal quickly. Touch the slide first to check before sliding down.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: One of the first playground slides was built in a park in Kettering, England, in 1922.

facts_and_myths.claim: Plastic slides never get hot in the sun.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Plastic slides heat up too, especially dark-colored ones, so always check first.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Waiting until the person ahead reaches the bottom helps everyone slide safely.

name: Swing Set
visual_anchor: Two children soaring on red swings hanging from a tall metal frame in a sunny playground, blue sky and green trees behind, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Seats that hang from chains or ropes
You go back and forth higher and higher
Pumping your legs keeps you moving
Works just like a pendulum on a clock

facts_and_myths.claim: A playground swing is a kind of pendulum.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Like a clock pendulum, it swings back and forth from a fixed point above.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Pumping your legs at just the right moments adds energy and sends you higher.

facts_and_myths.claim: Heavier riders take much longer to swing back and forth.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The time for one swing depends mostly on the chain length, not the rider's weight.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Staying well away from the front and back of moving swings helps everyone stay safe.

name: Seesaw
visual_anchor: Two smiling kids on opposite ends of a bright blue seesaw, one up high and one low, in a sunny playground, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Needs two riders to play
A long board balanced on a pivot in the middle
One end goes up while the other goes down
A simple machine called a lever

facts_and_myths.claim: A seesaw is a simple machine called a lever.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The board is the lever and the middle pivot is the fulcrum.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In some places, a seesaw is called a teeter-totter.

facts_and_myths.claim: Two kids must weigh the same to balance a seesaw.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The heavier rider can scoot closer to the middle to balance a lighter rider.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: This same balancing trick is how old-fashioned weighing scales work.

name: Sandbox
visual_anchor: A wooden sandbox filled with golden sand, colorful buckets, spades and a toy dump truck under a shady umbrella in a sunny backyard, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A low box or pit filled with sand
Kids dig, scoop and build in it
Often comes with buckets, shovels and toy trucks
A cover keeps it clean when no one is playing

facts_and_myths.claim: Covering a sandbox when it isn't used helps keep it clean.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A cover keeps out rain, leaves and animals looking for a place to dig.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Sand gardens in Boston in the 1880s are often called the first American playgrounds.

facts_and_myths.claim: All sand is made only from crushed seashells.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Most sand comes from rocks worn into tiny grains, though some beaches have shell sand.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Play sand is washed and sifted so it is soft and clean for digging.

name: Monkey Bars
visual_anchor: A determined child swinging hand over hand across bright green overhead bars above soft wood chips in a sunny playground, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Playground bars you cross while hanging
Shaped like a ladder laid flat up high
You swing from one rung to the next, hand over hand
Named after an animal famous for swinging through trees

facts_and_myths.claim: Wrapping your thumbs around the bar gives a safer grip.
facts_and_myths.explanation: With your thumb hooked under the bar, your hand is less likely to slip off.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Swinging arm over arm like this is called brachiation, the way gibbons travel.

facts_and_myths.claim: Crossing monkey bars only works your arms.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Your hands, shoulders, back and belly muscles all work together to swing you across.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Soft ground like wood chips or rubber mats under monkey bars helps cushion falls.

name: Merry-Go-Round
visual_anchor: Kids holding the handrails of a bright red and yellow round spinning platform in a sunny playground, gentle motion blur, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Flat round platform that spins around
Kids run alongside to push it, then hop on
Has handrails to hold onto
You feel pushed outward as it turns

facts_and_myths.claim: On a merry-go-round, the outer edge moves faster than the center.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The edge travels a bigger circle in the same time, so it moves faster.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Hold on tight and wait until it stops before hopping off.

facts_and_myths.claim: Sitting at the center makes you go the fastest.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The middle barely moves. The farther out you sit, the faster you whirl.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In Britain, a playground merry-go-round is often called a roundabout.

name: Jungle Gym
visual_anchor: A colorful dome of crisscrossing bars with kids climbing and waving from the top in a sunny playground, soft rubber ground below, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A playground frame made for climbing
Built from many bars joined in a big grid
Kids climb up, through and hang from it
First patented in the United States in 1920

facts_and_myths.claim: The jungle gym was patented by Sebastian Hinton in 1920.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Hinton designed a frame of bars that let children climb and explore like in a forest.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In Britain, a jungle gym is usually called a climbing frame.

facts_and_myths.claim: Playgrounds are safest with hard concrete under the climbing frames.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Soft surfaces like rubber, sand or wood chips help cushion falls much better.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Using both hands and one foot, or both feet and one hand, makes climbing steadier.

name: Trampoline
visual_anchor: A joyful child bouncing high on a round backyard trampoline with a tall safety net, blue sky and puffy clouds above, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: Springy surface that sends you bouncing
A stretchy mat held by springs on a frame
Many have a safety net around the edge
Became an Olympic sport in the year 2000

facts_and_myths.claim: Trampolining has been an Olympic sport since the 2000 Sydney Games.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Athletes perform flips and twists high in the air and are scored by judges.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The word trampoline comes from a Spanish word for diving board.

facts_and_myths.claim: More kids jumping at once makes a trampoline safer.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Bumping into each other causes many trampoline accidents. One jumper at a time is safest.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The modern trampoline was built in the 1930s by American gymnast George Nissen.

name: Treehouse
visual_anchor: A cozy wooden treehouse with a little window, rope ladder and bunting nestled in the branches of a big leafy oak, golden afternoon light, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A little hideout built up high
Sits among the branches of a big tree
Often reached by a rope ladder or wooden steps
Needs a strong, healthy tree to hold it safely

facts_and_myths.claim: Some treehouses are attached with special bolts that let the tree keep growing.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Builders use strong bolts and supports that leave room for the trunk and branches to grow.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Some hotels around the world let families sleep in treehouses among the branches.

facts_and_myths.claim: Any tree, even a young skinny one, can hold a treehouse.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A treehouse needs a big, healthy, mature tree. Ask an adult to check and build it.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Railings around a treehouse platform help keep everyone safe up high.

name: Zip Line
visual_anchor: A grinning child in a helmet and harness gliding along a cable above green treetops, sunny sky and mountains in the distance, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A ride where you glide along a cable
The cable runs from a high point to a lower one
Riders hang from a wheeled pulley called a trolley
Riders wear a harness and helmet for safety

facts_and_myths.claim: Gravity is what pulls riders along a zip line.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The cable slopes downhill, so gravity pulls the rider from the high end to the low end.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In rainforests like those in Costa Rica, zip lines let visitors glide above the treetops.

facts_and_myths.claim: Zip lines have a motor that pulls riders along.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Most zip lines have no motor. A slope, a pulley and gravity do the work.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Big zip lines use helmets, harnesses and trained guides to keep riders safe.

name: Bouncy Castle
visual_anchor: A giant inflatable castle in bright red, yellow and blue with puffy towers and kids bouncing inside at a sunny backyard party, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A puffy play castle filled with air
Kids take off their shoes and bounce inside
Often seen at birthday parties and fairs
A fan blows air into it the whole time

facts_and_myths.claim: A bouncy castle needs a fan blowing air into it the entire time.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Air slowly escapes through the seams, so the blower keeps refilling it.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Inflatable bouncers were first invented in the United States in 1959.

facts_and_myths.claim: Bouncy castles are safe to use in strong winds.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Wind can lift a bouncy castle, so it must be staked down and not used on very windy days.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Taking turns with kids of a similar size makes bouncing safer and more fun.

name: Splash Pad
visual_anchor: Laughing kids running through arcs of sparkling water shooting up from colorful ground jets and a giant tipping bucket, sunny summer day, 9:16 vertical shot.
core_traits: A wet play area for hot summer days
Water sprays up from jets in the ground
Often has fountains, sprinklers and tipping buckets
Has no deep pool of standing water

facts_and_myths.claim: Splash pads have no deep standing water to swim in.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Water sprays up and drains away right away, so the ground stays shallow.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Many splash pads clean and reuse their water, while others use fresh water.

facts_and_myths.claim: You must know how to swim to play at a splash pad.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Kids just run through sprays, so swimming isn't needed. An adult should still watch.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Water shoes and sunscreen help keep splash pad fun safe on hot days.
